hmmt-feb-2009-team1-01.title: Show the chromatic number is always 3
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-01.body:
**Claim:** every triangulation graph of a convex $n$-gon has chromatic number $3$. Since it contains a triangle, at least $3$ colors are needed. We show $3$ suffice by induction on $n$. For $n=3$ the graph is a triangle.

Let $n>3$. The $n-2$ triangles have $3(n-2)$ edge-slots in total; each side lies in exactly one triangle and each of the $n-3$ diagonals lies in exactly two, so the number of (triangle, side) incidences is $3(n-2)-2(n-3)=n$. Since there are only $n-2<n$ triangles, by pigeonhole some triangle contains two sides of the polygon. These two sides share a vertex $v$, so the triangle is $v$ and its two polygon neighbours $u,w$, with $uw$ a diagonal. The vertex $v$ is adjacent to nothing else (a diagonal from $v$ would have to enter the interior of this triangle and cross $uw$ or leave the polygon). Deleting $v$ leaves a triangulation of the convex $(n-1)$-gon with the diagonal $uw$ now a side. By induction color it with $3$ colors, then give $v$ a color different from those of its two neighbours $u,w$. This is a good $3$-coloring of the original graph. Hence the chromatic number is $3$ for every triangulation. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-02a.title: Parity of the number of prime factors
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-02a.body:
$v_1$ and $v_2$ are adjacent ($2/1$ is prime), so at least $2$ colors are needed. Let $f(n)$ be the number of prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity. If $v_a,v_b$ are adjacent with $a<b$, then $b=pa$ for a prime $p$, so $f(b)=f(a)+1$ has the opposite parity. So coloring $v_n$ red if $f(n)$ is odd and blue if even is a good $2$-coloring. The chromatic number is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-02b.title: Triangle plus mod 3
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-02b.body:
$v_0,v_1,v_2$ are pairwise adjacent (differences $1,1,2$ are powers of $2$), so at least $3$ colors are needed. Color $v_n$ by $n\bmod3$. If $v_a,v_b$ have the same color then $3\mid a-b$; but no power of $2$ is divisible by $3$, so they are not adjacent. Hence $3$ colors suffice.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-03a.title: Greedy coloring
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-03a.body: List the vertices $x_1,\dots,x_m$ and color them in order, giving each the smallest of the colors $1,\dots,k+1$ not used on an already-colored neighbour. Each vertex has only $k$ neighbours, so at most $k$ of the $k+1$ colors are blocked, and a free color always exists. The result is a good coloring with at most $k+1$ colors. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-03b.title: Induction on $n$
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-03b.body:
**Answer: $\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2$.** The complete graph $K_n$ has chromatic number $n$ and $\binom n2$ edges, so the minimum is at most $\binom n2$.

We prove by induction on $n$: every finite graph with chromatic number **at least** $n$ has at least $\binom n2$ edges. For $n=1$ this is trivial. Suppose it holds for $n$ and let $G$ have chromatic number at least $n+1$. If every vertex had degree at most $n-1$, then by part (a) (greedy coloring, which works for degree at most $k$) $G$ could be colored with $n$ colors, a contradiction. So some vertex $v$ has degree at least $n$. Remove $v$. The graph $G-v$ has chromatic number at least $n$: otherwise, color $G-v$ with at most $n-1$ colors and give $v$ a new color to get a coloring of $G$ with at most $n$ colors. By the induction hypothesis, $G-v$ has at least $\binom n2$ edges, so $G$ has at least $\binom n2+n=\binom{n+1}2$ edges. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-04a.title: The 5-cycle
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-04a.body: Take $5$ vertices $x_0,\dots,x_4$ in a circle, with $x_i$ adjacent exactly to $x_{i\pm1}$ (indices mod $5$). It has no triangle since no three vertices are pairwise adjacent. Two colors are impossible: the colors must alternate around the cycle, but going around an odd cycle returns to the start with the wrong color. Three colors suffice: color $x_0,\dots,x_4$ with $1,2,1,2,3$. So the chromatic number is $3$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-04b.title: Join with a new vertex
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-04b.body:
Induction on $n\ge3$: for each $n$ there is a graph with chromatic number $n$ and no $n$-clique. For $n=3$ use the $5$-cycle (part (a)).

Suppose $G$ has chromatic number $n$ and no $n$-clique. Let $G'$ be $G$ plus a new vertex $v$ adjacent to every vertex of $G$. In any good coloring of $G'$, the restriction to $G$ is a good coloring of $G$, so it uses at least $n$ colors, and $v$ is adjacent to all of $G$ so its color differs from all of them: at least $n+1$ colors. Conversely $G$ can be colored with $n$ colors and $v$ given a new color: $n+1$ colors suffice. So $\chi(G')=n+1$. If $G'$ contained an $(n+1)$-clique $K$, then $K\setminus\{v\}$ (or $K$ itself if $v\notin K$, in which case remove any vertex) would give an $n$-clique contained in $G$, contradiction. Hence $G'$ has chromatic number $n+1$ and no $(n+1)$-clique. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-05a.title: Odd cycle joined with a clique
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-05a.body:
Let $k\ge N$ be an odd number and $C_k$ the cycle on $k$ vertices; it has chromatic number $3$. Let $H=K_{n-3}$ (empty if $n=3$), and let $J$ be $C_k$ and $H$ together with all edges between a vertex of $C_k$ and a vertex of $H$. Then $J$ has $k+n-3\ge N$ vertices.

*$\chi(J)=n$:* the vertices of $H$ are adjacent to everything else, so their $n-3$ colors are all distinct from each other and from the colors used on $C_k$, which needs at least $3$ colors. So at least $n$ colors are needed, and $n-3$ colors for $H$ plus $3$ for $C_k$ suffice.

*Removing any vertex lowers $\chi$:* if the vertex is in $C_k$, the cycle becomes a path, which can be $2$-colored, so $J$ minus the vertex can be colored with $(n-3)+2=n-1$ colors. If the vertex is in $H$, then $H$ becomes $K_{n-4}$ and we need $(n-4)+3=n-1$ colors. (And $\chi\ge n-1$ always by the removal bound, but we only need that it is less than $n$.) So removing any vertex decreases the chromatic number. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-05b.title: Pigeonhole on a good $n$-coloring
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-05b.body: Take $N=nr$. Let $G$ have at least $nr$ vertices and chromatic number $n$, and fix a good $n$-coloring. By pigeonhole some color class contains at least $r$ vertices; choose $r$ of them. No two of these are adjacent. Remove these $r$ vertices and let $G'$ be the remaining graph. Suppose $G'$ could be colored with at most $n-2$ colors. Then give all $r$ removed vertices one new color: since they are pairwise non-adjacent, this gives a good coloring of $G$ with at most $n-1$ colors, contradicting $\chi(G)=n$. So $\chi(G')\ge n-1$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-06a.title: Product coloring and a matching construction
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-06a.body:
**Upper bound.** Take good colorings of $G$ with colors $1,\dots,a$ and of $H$ with colors $1,\dots,b$, and give each vertex the pair (its $G$-color, its $H$-color), one of $ab$ colors. If $x,y$ are adjacent in $G\cup H$, they are adjacent in $G$ or in $H$, so their $G$-colors or their $H$-colors differ, and so the pairs differ. Hence $\chi(G\cup H)\le ab$.

**Construction.** Let the vertices be the pairs $(i,j)$ with $1\le i\le a$, $1\le j\le b$. Let $G$ join $(i,j)$ and $(i',j)$ for $i\ne i'$ (so $G$ is $b$ disjoint copies of $K_a$, with $\chi(G)=a$), and let $H$ join $(i,j)$ and $(i',j')$ whenever $j\ne j'$ (a complete $b$-partite graph, with $\chi(H)=b$). Every two distinct vertices are adjacent in $G$ (same $j$) or in $H$ (different $j$), so $G\cup H=K_{ab}$ has chromatic number $ab$.

**Answer: $ab$** ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-06b.title: Iterate the product coloring
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-06b.body:
By the product-coloring argument, $\chi(A\cup B)\le\chi(A)\chi(B)$ for graphs on the same vertex set (give each vertex the pair of its colors in $A$ and in $B$). By induction, $\chi(G_1\cup\cdots\cup G_k)\le\prod\chi(G_i)\le2^k$. Since the union is $G$ with $\chi(G)=n$, we get $n\le2^k$, so $k\ge\log_2n$, and since $k$ is an integer, $k\ge\lceil\log_2n\rceil$. ∎

*(Remark: this is sharp: color $G$ with colors $1,\dots,n$ and let $G_i$ join two vertices of $G$ whenever the $i$-th binary digits of their colors differ; each $G_i$ is $2$-colorable by that digit, $\lceil\log_2n\rceil$ graphs suffice, and every edge of $G$ appears since adjacent vertices have different colors, hence differ in some digit.)*

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-07.title: Double counting a color class
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-07.body:
For a string $s$ let $T_s$ be the set of the $n+1$ strings that differ from $s$ in at most one place. Any two strings in $T_s$ differ in at most $2$ places, so $T_s$ is a clique of size $n+1$; hence $\chi(G_n)\ge n+1$ and in any good coloring with exactly $n+1$ colors, every color appears exactly once in each $T_s$.

Suppose there were a good $(n+1)$-coloring and fix a color $c$ used on $m$ vertices. Count pairs $(v,s)$ with $v$ colored $c$ and $v\in T_s$. Each such $v$ lies in $T_s$ for exactly $n+1$ strings $s$ (namely $v$ and its $n$ neighbours at distance $1$), giving $m(n+1)$ pairs. On the other hand each of the $2^n$ sets $T_s$ contains exactly one vertex colored $c$, giving $2^n$ pairs. So $m(n+1)=2^n$, hence $n+1\mid2^n$ and $n+1$ is a power of $2$, contrary to the assumption. So no $(n+1)$-coloring exists, and since $\chi(G_n)\ge n+1$, we get $\chi(G_n)\ge n+2$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2009-team1-08.title: Case analysis
hmmt-feb-2009-team1-08.body:
**$n=1$.** A graph with chromatic number $1$ has no edges and has exactly one coloring: $(1,1)$ only.

**$n=2$.** The graph has an edge and is bipartite. Each connected component (with at least one vertex) has exactly two good colorings with two colors, because the color of one vertex forces the colors of all vertices in the component. If there are $c$ components, there are $2^c$ colorings and $2^{c-1}$ up to relabeling. Every $c\ge1$ occurs (take $c$ disjoint edges). So $k=2^{c-1}$: exactly the pairs $(2,2^j)$, $j\ge0$.

**$n>2$, any $k\ge1$.** Start with the clique $K_n$ on $v_1,\dots,v_n$ (only one coloring up to relabeling, each $v_i$ having its own color $c_i$); this is the whole graph if $k=1$. For $k>1$ add vertices $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$ with edges $w_iw_{i+1}$ ($1\le i\le k-2$), and join:
- $w_i$ with $i\equiv0\pmod3$ to all $v_j$ except $v_1,v_2$,
- $w_i$ with $i\equiv1\pmod3$ to all $v_j$ except $v_2,v_3$,
- $w_i$ with $i\equiv2\pmod3$ to all $v_j$ except $v_1,v_3$.

The chromatic number is still $n$ since $K_n$ forces $n$ colors and the $w_i$ can take colors of the clique. In a good $n$-coloring, $w_i$ must take one of the two colors of its two non-neighbours in the clique: $\{c_1,c_2\}$, $\{c_2,c_3\}$, $\{c_1,c_3\}$ for the three residue classes. Consecutive sets share exactly one color; let $s_i$ be the color shared by the sets of $w_i$ and $w_{i+1}$ (the pattern repeats with period $3$, so define also $s_0$ and $s_{k-1}$ by continuing it). Then the set of $w_i$ is exactly $\{s_{i-1},s_i\}$ with $s_{i-1}\ne s_i$ (check: $w_1:\{c_2,c_3\}$, $s_1=c_3$, $w_2:\{c_3,c_1\}$, $s_2=c_1$, $w_3:\{c_1,c_2\}$, $s_3=c_2$, and so on). Call $w_i$ *low* if it gets color $s_{i-1}$ and *high* if it gets color $s_i$. Adjacent $w_i,w_{i+1}$ may not get the same color, and the only color available to both is $s_i$, so the only forbidden pattern is "$w_i$ high and $w_{i+1}$ low". Therefore a good coloring is a sequence $\text{low},\dots,\text{low},\text{high},\dots,\text{high}$, determined by the number $j\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ of lows. That gives exactly $k$ good colorings; they are pairwise distinct as partitions because they differ in which clique color a given $w_i$ takes. Hence exactly $k$ distinct good colorings with $n$ colors. ∎
